name: THE THOUSAND CHARD STARE BURGER (comes with thousand island dressing and swiss chard)

recipe.history:
Swiss chard — Beta vulgaris subsp. cicla — is native to the Mediterranean basin and has been cultivated since antiquity, with evidence of its use in ancient Greece and Rome, where it was valued both as food and medicine. Despite its common name, Swiss chard is not particularly Swiss — it is believed the nineteenth-century botanist W.D.J. Koch gave it the designation to distinguish it from French-named varieties, and the name stuck. Its vivid rainbow stems — deep red, golden yellow, white — have made it a garden staple across temperate climates worldwide, and its leaves, which combine the mild earthiness of beet greens with a slight metallic mineral quality reminiscent of spinach, make it one of the most versatile cooking greens available. In Mediterranean cooking, chard is braised with olive oil and garlic, stuffed into pastries, cooked into soups, and eaten raw in salads, reflecting thousands of years of culinary creativity around a single adaptable plant.

Thousand Island dressing has a more contested and thoroughly American origin. The most widely accepted story places its creation in the early twentieth century in the Thousand Islands region of the Saint Lawrence River at the border of upstate New York and Ontario, where a fishing guide's wife named Sophia LaLonde reportedly made the dressing for her husband's shore dinners and actress May Irwin brought the recipe to the maitre d' of the Waldorf-Astoria in New York City, who put it on the menu and named it after the region. By the 1910s it was in commercial production, and by the mid-twentieth century it had become one of the best-selling salad dressings in America, as inseparable from the Reuben sandwich as from the iceberg wedge. The combination of mayonnaise, ketchup, sweet relish, and hard-boiled egg creates a sauce that is simultaneously sweet, tangy, creamy, and oddly complex — and its application to a burger with wilted Swiss chard creates a strange and wonderful harmony between American convenience food culture and Mediterranean vegetable tradition.

I began making Thousand Island from scratch after a dinner at which someone served a commercially bottled version and I found it both too sweet and somehow also too sour — a combination I had not known was possible in a condiment. Making it yourself, you discover that the balance is delicate: the ketchup's sweetness and acidity, the mayonnaise's fat and egg, the relish's sugar and vinegar, the hard-boiled egg's sulfurous creaminess — all of these need to be in a specific ratio or the whole thing tips in one direction and becomes a caricature. I spent three afternoons adjusting proportions before I found a version that tasted, to me, like the best possible version of itself: creamy without being heavy, sweet without being cloying, tangy without being sharp. The chard, wilted quickly with garlic and a splash of vinegar, adds a minerality that cuts through the richness of the dressing in a way that no other green quite manages.

Medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is the temperature that allows Thousand Island dressing to function as it should on a burger. The sauce, applied cold to the warm bun, begins to thin slightly as it contacts the heat radiating from the patty, flowing into the crevices of the bread and seasoning the whole interior of the sandwich evenly. This effect requires the patty to be genuinely warm at its surface but not desiccated — a medium rare interior means the exterior has a crust of appropriate temperature, warm enough to gently loosen the sauce, pink enough to provide the moisture that prevents the dressing from overwhelming the meat. A well-done patty sits at the center of a burger and contributes nothing but heat and density. A medium rare patty is a participant.
ingredients: 3 large eggs (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
For the homemade Thousand Island dressing:
Salt and white pepper to taste
For the wilted Swiss chard with garlic:
2 large bunches rainbow Swiss chard, stems and leaves separated
900g freshly ground beef (80% chuck, 20% brisket blend)
1 medium red onion, sliced into thin rings
instructions: 1. Make the Thousand Island dressing: Combine mayonnaise, ketchup, sweet pickle relish, finely chopped hard-boiled egg, white wine vinegar, Worcestershire sauce, granulated sugar, and smoked paprika in a medium bowl. Stir until thoroughly combined. Season with salt and white pepper. Taste and adjust — the dressing should be creamy, mildly sweet, and gently tangy. Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes for the flavors to meld.

2. Wilt the Swiss chard: Wash the chard thoroughly. Slice the stems into 1cm pieces and roughly chop the leaves, keeping them separate. Heat olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add garlic slices and red pepper flakes and cook, stirring, for 60 seconds until fragrant and just beginning to golden. Add the chard stems and cook for 3–4 minutes until they begin to soften. Add the chard leaves and apple cider vinegar, toss, and cook for 2–3 more minutes until the leaves are fully wilted but still bright and slightly textured. Season with salt and pepper. Set aside.

3. Make the brioche buns: Combine bread flour, instant yeast, salt, and sugar in a stand mixer with a dough hook. Add 2 eggs and warm milk, mix on low for 2 minutes, then knead on medium for 5 minutes. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time. Knead on medium-high for 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.

4. Place dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 hour until doubled. Divide into 6 portions of about 100g, shape into tight balls, and proof on parchment-lined baking sheets, covered, for 45 minutes.
5. Preheat oven to 190°C (375°F). Brush buns with egg wash (remaining egg plus 1 tablespoon water) and bake for 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.

6. Form the beef patties: Divide ground beef into 6 equal portions of 150g. Handle minimally. Form into 10cm-wide, 2cm-thick patties with a thumb indent in the center. Season both sides generously with salt and cracked pepper immediately before cooking.

7. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties dry and undisturbed for 3 minutes. Flip once. Place a slice of Swiss (Emmentaler) cheese on each patty immediately. Cook for 2–2.5 more minutes. Confirm the center reads 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a wire rack for 3 minutes.
8. Slice brioche buns and toast cut-side down in a buttered skillet over medium heat for 60–90 seconds.

9. Assemble each burger: Spread Thousand Island dressing generously on both cut faces of the bun. Place shredded iceberg lettuce and tomato slices on the bottom bun. Add red onion rings. Set the rested Swiss cheese-topped patty on top. Pile a generous portion of the wilted garlic chard on top of the patty. Finish with flaky sea salt and the top bun. Serve with extra Thousand Island dressing on the side.
